content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'love' (Greek agape) primarily signifies the essential nature and character of God himself and the self-giving, sacrificial disposition God shows toward humanity, supremely revealed in Christ's death; derivatively it names the chief covenant obligation of believers — wholehearted love of God and neighbor — which sums up and fulfills the entire law and is the distinguishing mark of Christian discipleship. It is typically distinguished from mere emotion or desire and defined as willed, active, self-donating benevolence.", "primary_basis": ["1 John 4:7-21 (esp. 'God is love', vv. 8, 16)", "John 3:16", "Romans 5:8", "John 15:13", "1 Corinthians 13:1-13", "Matthew 22:37-40 (citing Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18)", "Mark 12:28-31", "John 13:34-35", "Romans 13:8-10", "Galatians 5:22 (love as first fruit of the Spirit)", "Ephesians 5:1-2, 25", "1 John 3:16-18"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Covenant loyalty / steadfast love (Hebrew hesed): love understood chiefly as faithful, binding covenant commitment between God and Israel rather than affection — prominent in Old Testament scholarship and biblical theology.", "basis": ["Exodus 34:6-7", "Deuteronomy 7:7-9", "Psalm 136 (refrain 'his steadfast love endures forever')", "Hosea 2:19-20", "Lamentations 3:22-23", "Micah 6:8"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Nuptial or bridal-mystical love: love as the symbol of the union between God/Christ and the soul or the Church, developed allegorically from the Song of Songs and marriage imagery — central in patristic, medieval, and mystical traditions (Origen, Bernard of Clairvaux, John of the Cross).", "basis": ["Song of Songs (read allegorically, e.g., 1:2; 2:16; 8:6-7)", "Hosea 1-3", "Ephesians 5:25-32", "Revelation 19:7-9; 21:2", "Isaiah 62:5"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Trinitarian-ontological reading: love as the inner relational life of the Trinity, with the Holy Spirit understood as the bond of love between Father and Son (Augustine, Richard of St. Victor) — a theological rather than strictly exegetical tradition.", "basis": ["John 17:24-26", "1 John 4:8, 16", "Romans 5:5", "John 3:35; 5:20"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Ethical-practical/social reading: love defined primarily as concrete action toward the poor, the enemy, and the marginalized — love of neighbor as the operational test of faith, emphasized in social-gospel, Anabaptist, and liberationist interpretation.", "basis": ["Matthew 25:31-46", "Luke 10:25-37 (Good Samaritan)", "Matthew 5:43-48 (love of enemies)", "James 2:14-17", "1 John 3:17-18"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Lexical multi-type schema: 'love' parsed into distinct kinds (agape, philia, eros, storge), popularized by C. S. Lewis and by claims of a sharp agape/eros contrast (Nygren); modern lexical scholarship treats the sharp word-distinctions as overstated.", "basis": ["John 21:15-17 (agapao/phileo interchange)", "1 Corinthians 13", "Song of Songs (eros)", "Anders Nygren, Agape and Eros; C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (interpretive tradition, not scripture)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Love reduced to sentiment or unconditional affirmation without moral demand — a popular-level usage generally rejected in formal Christian teaching, which ties love to obedience and holiness.", "basis": ["John 14:15 ('If you love me, keep my commandments' — cited against this reading)", "1 John 5:3", "Hebrews 12:6 (love includes discipline)"], "prominence": "rare"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "'Love' is less a symbol pointing to something else than a core theological concept, but its interpretive consensus is unusually strong: God's own nature and self-giving action in Christ, and the summary command governing Christian life. The main interpretive variations (hesed covenant loyalty, bridal mysticism, Trinitarian bond, social-ethical emphasis) are complementary strands within the tradition rather than rival meanings. Debates exist over the agape/eros distinction and whether Greek word choices carry the weight sometimes claimed, but these do not disturb the broad consensus."}
